title: Hypothesis: Types, Directional and Non-Directional
summary: Definition of hypothesis; null (H0) and alternate hypothesis; one-tailed vs two-tailed tests; directional vs non-directional hypotheses.
objectives: Match hypothesis type to one-tailed or two-tailed test.
revision: H₀ = no effect; H₁ = effect. Directional → one-tailed; non-directional → two-tailed.
traps: The null hypothesis always contains equality (=, ≤, or ≥).
confusions: Believing the null hypothesis is what the researcher wants to prove.

notes.t: A tentative statement or assumption made about a population parameter, which can be tested using statistical methods.

r: No effect or no difference; represents the status quo.
There is an effect or a difference; what the researcher hopes to support.

i: Directional (one-tailed): specifies the direction of the effect (greater than or less than).
Non-directional (two-tailed): does not specify direction; tests for an effect in both directions.

notes.t: A one-tailed test is used when the research hypothesis specifies a direction of the effect. A two-tailed test is used when the research hypothesis does not specify a direction and tests for the possibility of an effect in both directions.
Null hypothesis (H₀) states no effect/no difference. Directional hypotheses use one-tailed tests; non-directional use two-tailed. Frequently tested in UGC NET.

One-tailed tests place the entire rejection region in one tail of the distribution (used when the hypothesis specifies a direction). Two-tailed tests split the rejection region across both tails (used when no direction is specified).

mnemonics.title: NULL vs ALT
mnemonics.text: NULL = No effect / No difference / Status quo. ALT = Effect exists / Difference exists / Researcher's claim.
